text:
Moth and Gravel Field Note 15
Cancelled is a result. An AI

narrated edition of the
published note.

You start a scan of a large
folder. A minute in, you change

your mind and press cancel. The
progress disappears. What did

you just get? Nothing, most
screens would say. The scan did

not finish, but something did
happen. The work began, stopped,

and left the world in some
state. Nothing is a claim about

that state, and it is rarely
checked.

Three small tools on our bench
answer differently. Each treats

the unhappy ending as a result
of its own. The scan that did

not finish, Verstas, is a
prototype that looks at the

workspaces on a disk and plans
their cleanup. It only looks and

plans. It deletes nothing. For
each thing it might clean, the

plan gives one of three answers:
ready, review required, or

blocked. In a recorded run on a
synthetic tree of 240,012 files,

a scan was cancelled during
discovery. The desktop said so

in plain words. The operation
was cancelled before

finalization. Every live
progress region cleared. The

inventory from the last finished
scan stayed selected instead of

being replaced by half of a new
one. The same banner at reading

size. The identifiers belong to
the synthetic run. The finished

history gained no entry for the
cancelled scan.

The next scan finished normally,
and only its final answer

replaced the earlier inventory.
The scan after the cancellation

finalized. Unaltered crop from
the same recorded run. The

identifiers and times are the
run's own. The important part is

what did not happen. The
cancelled scan did not become a

small, plausible inventory. A
partial count is easy to mistake

for a complete one, especially
in a tool whose next step might

be, clean these up. The step
that failed. Luozi drives

Android devices from a laptop,
one step at a time. When a step

fails, the run does not end in a
red line and silence. It writes

a failure envelope. Which
scenario? Which step? What the

step was doing? The error and
its kind? And the screenshot,

recording, and log it kept. The
record itself is shown on the

page. A shortened excerpt from a
failure envelope in Luozi's test

fixtures. A fixture, not a
recorded device run. Ellipses

mark omissions. A failure
becomes something to read later,

after the device is unplugged.
Failed at step two, watching the

stream, a transport error,
starts a different conversation

from it didn't work. The machine
that went quiet. The third tool

is smaller. A relay bridge of
ours connects a relay board to a

message broker, so a laptop can
switch its outputs. When the

bridge connects, it announces
that it is online. Before that,

it leaves the broker a last
will. The code itself is shown

on the page. From the bridge's
source, with its comment

shortened. Read from the code,
no hardware run was made for

this note. If the bridge
disappears without saying

goodbye, the broker publishes
offline on its behalf, and keeps

it for anyone who asks later.
Silence would be easier to

build, but it is also ambiguous.
Quiet could mean nothing

changed, or that nobody is left
to say so. A retained offline

turns a disappearance into a
message with a time on it. The

last will covers only the
connection. Whether a relay

actually switched is a separate
question. After a command, the

bridge tries to read the relay
state back from the board and

reports what it read. One habit
serves. One habit serves three

tools and surfaces. The unhappy
path leaves a receipt. The

receipt is shown in the same
place as success, in the same

plain voice, and it does not
claim more than it knows. For

any button that starts something
long or destructive, there is a

useful question to ask before
shipping it. What does the

screen say if you stop halfway?
If the answer is nothing, a

result is probably missing. What
these endings show. The Verstas

images are unaltered crops from
a recorded Windows run of the

prototype at a pinned source
revision on a synthetic file

tree. The tool planned only.
Nothing was deleted. Verstas is

a working name. The Luozi
envelope is shortened from a

test fixture, not from a device
run. The relay bridge lines are

read from its source. No
hardware run was made for this

note. No study with people was
run. Whether someone reads these

endings as results is the next
question. Read the image and

source provenance. You have been
listening to Moth and Gravel

Field Notes. The written edition
is at mothandgravel.com.
